{{Short description|Concept in computability theory}}
In [[computability theory]], the '''T predicate''', first studied by mathematician [[Stephen Cole Kleene]], is a particular [[ternary relation|set of triples]] of [[natural number]]s that is used to represent [[computable function]]s within [[theory (mathematical logic)|formal theories]] of [[arithmetic]]. Informally, the ''T'' predicate tells whether a particular [[computer program]] will halt when run with a particular input, and the corresponding ''U'' function is used to obtain the results of the computation if the program does halt. As with the [[Smn theorem|s<sub>mn</sub> theorem]], the original notation used by Kleene has become standard terminology for the concept.<ref>The predicate described here was presented in (Kleene 1943) and (Kleene 1952), and this is what is usually called "Kleene's ''T'' predicate".  (Kleene 1967) uses the letter ''T'' to describe a different predicate related to computable functions, but which cannot be used to obtain Kleene's normal form theorem.</ref>

== Definition ==
[[File:KleeneT collatz5.gif|thumb|901px|Example call of ''T''<sub>1</sub>. The {{background color|#e0e0ff|1st argument}} gives the source code (in [[C (programming language)|C]] rather than as a [[Gödel number]] ''e'') of a computable function, viz. the [[Collatz conjecture|Collatz function]] ''f''. The {{background color|#ffe0e0|2nd argument}} gives the natural number ''i''  to which ''f'' is to be applied. The {{background color|#e0ffe0|3rd argument}} gives a sequence ''x'' of computation steps simulating the evaluation of ''f'' on ''i'' (as an equation chain rather than a Gödel sequence number). The predicate call evaluates to ''true'' since ''x'' is actually the correct computation sequence for the call ''f''(5), and ends with an expression not involving ''f'' anymore. The function ''U'', applied to the sequence ''x'', will return its final expression, viz. 1.]]
<!-- todo: introduce some notation to make this easier -->
The definition depends on a suitable [[Gödel numbering]] that assigns natural numbers to [[computable function]]s (given as [[Turing machine]]s). This numbering must be sufficiently effective that, given an index of a computable function and an input to the function, it is possible to effectively simulate the computation of the function on that input.  The <math>T</math> predicate is obtained by formalizing this simulation.

The [[ternary relation]] <math>T_1(e,i,x)</math> takes three natural numbers as arguments. <math>T_1(e,i,x)</math> is true if <math>x</math> encodes a computation history of the computable function with index <math>e</math> when run with input <math>i</math>, and the program halts as the last step of this computation history. That is, 
* <math>T_1</math> first asks whether <math>x</math> is the [[Gödel numbering for sequences|Gödel number]] of a finite sequence <math>\langle x_{j} \rangle</math> of complete configurations of the Turing machine with index <math>e</math>, running a computation on input <math>i</math>.  
* If so, <math>T_1</math> then asks if this sequence begins with the starting state of the computation and each successive element of the sequence corresponds to a single step of the Turing machine. 
* If it does, <math>T_1</math> finally asks whether the sequence <math>\langle x_{j} \rangle</math> ends with the machine in a halting state. 
If all three of these questions have a positive answer, then <math>T_1(e,i,x)</math> is true, otherwise, it is false.

The <math>T_1</math> predicate is [[primitive recursive]] in the sense that there is a primitive recursive function that, given inputs for the predicate, correctly determines the [[truth value]] of the predicate on those inputs. 

There is a corresponding primitive recursive function <math>U</math> such that if <math>T_1(e,i,x)</math> is true then <math>U(x)</math> returns the output of the function with index <math>e</math> on input <math>i</math>.

Because Kleene's formalism attaches a number of inputs to each function, the predicate <math>T_1</math> can only be used for functions that take one input. There are additional predicates for functions with multiple inputs; the relation

:<math>T_k(e, i_1, \ldots, i_k, x)</math>

is true if <math>x</math> encodes a halting computation of the function with index <math>e</math> on the inputs <math>i_1,\ldots,i_k</math>.

Like <math>T_1</math>, all functions <math>T_k</math> are primitive recursive.
Because of this, any theory of arithmetic that is able to represent every primitive recursive function is able to represent <math>T</math> and <math>U</math>. Examples of such arithmetical theories include [[Robinson arithmetic]] and stronger theories such as [[Peano arithmetic]].

== Normal form theorem ==

The <math>T_k</math> predicates can be used to obtain '''Kleene's normal form theorem''' for computable functions (Soare 1987, p.&nbsp;15; Kleene 1943, p.&nbsp;52&mdash;53). This states there exists a fixed [[primitive recursive function]] <math>U</math> such that a function <math>f:\mathbb{N}^{k}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}</math> is computable [[if and only if]] there is a number <math>e</math> such that for all <math>n_1,\ldots,n_k</math> one has
:<math>f(n_1,\ldots,n_k) \simeq U( \mu x\, T_k(e,n_1,\ldots,n_k,x))</math>,
where ''&mu;'' is the [[mu operator|''&mu;'' operator]] (<math>\mu x\, \phi(x)</math> is the smallest natural number for which <math>\phi(x)</math> is true) and <math>\simeq</math> is true if both sides are undefined or if both are defined and they are equal. By the theorem, the definition of every [[general recursive function]] ''f'' can be rewritten into a normal form such that the ''&mu;'' operator is used only once, viz. immediately below the topmost <math>U</math>, which is independent of the computable function <math>f</math>.

== Arithmetical hierarchy ==

In addition to encoding computability, the ''T'' predicate can be used to generate [[Turing complete set|complete sets]] in the [[arithmetical hierarchy]]. In particular, the set 
:<math> K = \{ e \mbox{ } : \mbox{ } \exists x T_1(e,0,x) \}</math>

which is of the same [[Turing degree]] as the [[halting problem]], is a <math>\Sigma^0_1</math> complete unary relation (Soare 1987, pp.&nbsp;28, 41). More generally, the set
:<math>K_{n+1} = \{ \langle e, a_1, \ldots, a_n\rangle : \exists x T_n(e, a_1, \ldots, a_n, x)\}</math> 
is a <math>\Sigma^0_1</math>-complete (''n''+1)-ary predicate. Thus, once a representation of the ''T''<sub>''n''</sub> predicate is obtained in a theory of arithmetic, a representation of a <math>\Sigma^0_1</math>-complete predicate can be obtained from it.

This construction can be extended higher in the arithmetical hierarchy, as in [[Post's theorem]] (compare Hinman 2005, p.&nbsp;397). For example, if a set <math>A \subseteq \mathbb{N}^{k+1}</math> is <math>\Sigma^0_{n}</math> complete then the set
:<math>\{ \langle a_1, \ldots, a_k\rangle : \forall x ( \langle a_1, \ldots, a_k, x\rangle \in A)\}</math>
is <math>\Pi^0_{n+1}</math> complete.
